newsitem.title: FRANCE: French spokesman quashes electoral law report.
newsitem.headline: French spokesman quashes electoral law report.

text.p: French cabinet spokesman Alain Lamassoure denied on Sunday that the government intended to reform electoral laws in time for general elections in 1998.
The bombshell reform suggestion, attributed to Prime Minister Alain Juppe and confirmed by aides, could have meant big gains for extreme rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen.
"There is no government plan to modify electoral laws in time for the general election," Lamassoure told RTL radio.
He said the subject came up last week during a meeting between Juppe and parliamentarians where the premier "mused aloud whether electoral laws might indeed be changed."
"But we went no further. This is not a government project, it's just an issue for political parties," Lamassoure said.
His statement came after a flurry of excitement over the possibility that some proportional representation might be re-introduced into the French electoral system.

The main -- and probably intended -- effect would be that the opposition Socialists would lose dozens of seats they expect to win from the right to junior partners on their own left, political analysts say.
But it would also mean the likely election to the 577-seat National Assembly of up to 40 members from Le Pen's stridently-xenophobic National Front (FN), they believe.
Polls suggest Gaullist President Jacques Chirac's failure to fulfil promises of lower unemployment and better living standards will give the opposition a strong boost.

The reform proposal had been coolly greeted at the weekend by leaders of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF) party, before which Juppe made a call for unity in the Atlantic resort of La Baule on Saturday.
The UDF is junior partner in the conservative cabinet led by the neo-Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party from whose ranks both Chirac and Juppe emerged.
Culture Minister Jacques Toubon, a Juppe loyalist, said the reform would introduce a measure of fairness into French politics where minority views were shut out of parliament.

But French Jewish leader Henri Hajdenberg, to whose community Le Pen is anathema, slammed the reform suggestion, saying: "Who will believe the change has any goal other than to preserve their (RPR) interests even if those who will benefit will be the National Front? We are fiercely opposed."
Under the current system, a candidate must win more than half the votes in the first round to be elected outright to the assembly. Otherwise the two top candidates go on to a run-off.
The system allows for deals between mainstream left-wing and right-wing parties, especially beneficial to the Socialists, but it shuts out the FN, shunned by mainstream politicians.

The FN failed to win a single seat in the last national elections in 1993, despite winning 12.5 percent of the popular vote. The party, which wants to expel foreigners from France, is now credited with around 15 percent of voting intentions.
